name: Sandawe
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

catalog_locator: HHE 2008 sec. 4.3.5 'Reduplications and borrowings', p. 51 (header '51'); Eaton 2010 sec. 1.3 Phonological overview, p. 10; Steeman 2012 sec. 2.4 Tone, p. 37 and sec. 2.4.4, p. 48; Elderkin 1989 Abstract, p. viii.
catalog_quote: [HHE 2008 p. 51] The assignment of tone to Swahili borrowings in Sandawe shows a tendency for translating the stressed penultimate syllable in Swahili into a high toned syllable in Sandawe. The preceding and following tones are assigned low tone. Thus a word such as kijiji ‘village’, in which the second syllable is stressed, becomes /kìdʒídʒî/ L-H-L. [Eaton 2010 p. 10] Sandawe has two underlying tone levels: high /´/ and low /`/. A low tone preceded by a high tone causes the tone of any following high tone to be downstepped and occur as a mid tone on the surface level. [Steeman 2012 p. 37] Tone is constant in noun and verb roots, except for a few derivational suffixes that change the tone pattern of the root (e.g. the deverbal marker -ó, section 3.4.2). The tone system is based on two level tones, high (´) and low (`), and the rising contour tone . ... In the description, the syllable will be taken as the basic tone bearing unit. [Elderkin 1989 p. viii] It uses pitch in lexical items in such a way as allows it to be analysed as tone. The mora has a twofold function as a unit of length and a tone bearing unit. Each mora either has a high or a low tone. Downstep and downdrift occur. Each word is characterised by a range of pitch relative to the other words in an utterance. These ranges are analysed as tone levels. The use of tone levels is determined by syntactic structure and by the structure of the information.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Sandawe is described purely as a lexical tone language (underlying H vs L on morae/syllables, with downstep, tone spread and largely predictable tone melodies); none of the five accessible primary descriptions posits word stress or an accent position. The only stress remark is that Swahili penultimate stress is borrowed as a Sandawe high tone.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Kagaya 1993 (intro) notes the vowel of a word-initial syllable tends to be lengthened in isolation forms; Elderkin 1989 and Steeman 2012 describe word-level pitch registers ('word levels') assigned by syntax/information structure, not stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone statements concern the phonological word (root/stem plus suffixes and clitics); downdrift applies within the phonological word (Steeman 2012 p. 48). No citation-form stress domain is defined because no stress is described.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Sandawe (sand1273, ISO sad). Hunziker, Hunziker & Eaton 2008 is based mainly on one speaker from Magambua (western dialect); Eaton 2010 and Steeman 2012 draw on both western and eastern dialect speakers. No separate dialect glottocodes involved.

new_statements.quote: [sec. 1.2, PDF p. 4] The following tone markings are used: [a-acute] high, [a-grave] low, [a-hacek] rising, [a-circumflex] falling, [grave] floating low tone. [...] [sec. 4.2, PDF p. 14] That is, the verb occurs with a low tone pattern and contrasts with the high tone pattern of the immediately preceding focused constituent. new_statements.relation_note: Consistent with the existing statement from Hunziker, Hunziker & Eaton 2008 / Eaton 2010 (two underlying tone levels H and L with downstep; tone language, no stress statement). Eaton 2005 uses the same SIL (Hunziker & Hunziker) analysis, marks H/L plus rising/falling contours and a floating L, and likewise says nothing about stress. The catalog record itself has an empty rule (world-2026-09-17), so nothing is contradicted; this work adds no stress placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The paper is a syntax/information-structure study (focus marking by inflection, constituent order and tone). Its phonological preliminaries give consonant and vowel charts and a tone transcription with high, low, rising, falling and floating low tones; lexical stems and affixes carry 'basic tone patterns', verb tone patterns can be neutralised to all-low, and focus is signalled partly by tone/pitch ('prominence' is used only in the information-structure sense, realised as the focused constituent having the highest pitch). The words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur anywhere in the 27 pages; nothing is said about word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: none (no stress statement); tonal detail only: nasal vowels phonologically long; realis uninflected verbs neutralise to all-low tone except under certain conditions; sentence-initial irrealis verb must keep its underlying tone pattern.
new_statements.identity_note: Data from a single main consultant, Nestori Michaeli of Magambua, Usandawe (Kondoa district), collected June-September 2000; no dialect distinction is drawn. The PDF read is the author's preprint of the OPiL 1 paper (a selection from her 2002 Reading PhD thesis 'A grammar of focus in Sandawe'), unpaginated.

tone_statements.citation: Eaton, Helen. 2006. Sandawe (Illustrations of the IPA). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 36(2): 235-242. Cambridge University Press.
tone_statements.quote: Sandawe has two underlying tone levels: high, /´/, and low, /`/. A surface mid tone [ˉ] is analyzed as a downstepped high. High and low tones occur on both short and long vowels, although low-toned long vowels are rare. Rising tones (on long vowels only) and falling tones (on short and long vowels) occur and are analyzed as sequences of level tones. Word-final low tones fall slightly. ... Rightward tone spread occurs in non-word-final morae.
tone_statements.summary: Two underlying level tones H and L; surface mid = downstepped H; rising (long V only) and falling contours = H/L sequences; rightward tone spread over morae; tone-to-word association lexical; all-L tone lowering in genitive heads, verbs etc. Nothing on stress. 14+ tone-marked forms.

tone.quote: In this section, I discuss focus and its effect on phonological phrasing in Sandawe, a Khoisan language spoken in Tanzania (see Elderkin 1989 and Kagaya 1993 for discussion). Sandawe shows downstep, or a downward shift of pitch level, between words within a phonological phrase (see Pulleyblank 1986 for an analysis of downstep). ... (i) The p-phrase initial High tone is realized at the pitch level that is the same as that of the High tone of the last word in the immediately preceding p-phrase.
